Batched inference with structured prompt templates typically involves many requests that share a common prefix — a system prompt, few-shot examples, or a retrieval-augmented context block — followed by divergent per-request suffixes. The central question is: under what conditions does prefix caching actually reduce compute, and when does the bookkeeping overhead (cache lookup, eviction policy, invalidation signaling) eat the savings? The key concepts are the KV-cache (the materialized attention keys and values for already-processed tokens), prefix hashing (how runtimes fingerprint shared prefixes to decide what to reuse), and the collision/invalidation boundary (what happens when two requests share most but not all of a prefix, or when a template has a dynamic field injected mid-prefix). What a beginner misses is that prefix sharing isn't binary: a single dynamic field — a timestamp, a user ID, even a capitalization difference — injected before the stable portion of the template breaks the hash match and forces a full recompute from that token forward, making the "shared" prefix worthless for caching despite 95% token overlap. Experts also worry about cache thrashing under high concurrency: if the batch scheduler doesn't co-locate requests with matching prefixes onto the same device memory space, you pay repeated KV-recompute costs that look like a cache miss storm, and the diagnostic signal (GPU utilization stays high, latency doesn't drop) is easily misread as a hardware bottleneck rather than a scheduling failure.

Because transformer attention is causal, the KV-cache for token i depends only on tokens 0…i-1, so a dynamic field at position k invalidates the cache for all tokens from k onward — meaning you can reuse at most k/N of the prefix KV work, and the remaining (N-k)/N must be recomputed from scratch on every request. If k is near the end of the prefix (say, a user name injected at position 900 of a 1000-token system prompt), you reuse ~90% of the KV computation; if it's near the start (a per-user instruction modifier at position 50), you throw away nearly everything. This is the core insight behind RadixAttention in the SGLang paper (Zheng et al., 2024), which represents the KV-cache as a radix tree so that the longest common prefix across concurrent requests is automatically identified and the cache is split exactly at the first divergence point. The practical implication is a clear template design rule: push all dynamic fields as late (as far right) as possible in the prefix, ideally into the suffix, and front-load all static content — system instructions, persona definitions, retrieved documents, few-shot examples — so they form one long stable root that every request in the batch can share. Systems like vLLM (with its prefix-aware block allocator) and TensorRT-LLM both exploit this: they hash contiguous token blocks of fixed size (commonly 16 or 32 tokens), so a dynamic field doesn't just invalidate from position k — it invalidates the entire block containing k, meaning even a field at position k=31 in a 32-token block wastes the whole block. The corollary engineers often miss: if you have multiple dynamic fields, their ordering matters more than their count — two fields where the earlier one is at position 800 and the later at 900 is far better than the reverse, and restructuring templates to sort dynamic fields by their position (latest-varying last) can recover substantial cache hit rate without changing the semantic content of the prompt at all.

The canonical mitigation is dynamic field alignment: you pad the static content preceding a dynamic field with neutral tokens (spaces, a repeated separator, or a no-op instruction fragment) so the dynamic field begins exactly at a block boundary — position k = 0 mod B where B is the block size. This guarantees the poisoned block contains only dynamic content, and every preceding block remains fully cacheable; vLLM's prefix caching documentation explicitly notes that users should align prompt structure to page boundaries (their default page size is 16 tokens) to maximize KV-page reuse. The cost is straightforward: you add up to B-1 padding tokens to the prompt, which slightly increases attention FLOPS quadratically — for a 1000-token prefix with B=16, worst-case padding is 15 tokens, adding roughly 3% to prefix attention cost, which is almost always worth it given that a misaligned dynamic field can waste hundreds of tokens of KV recompute. A subtler strategy is field consolidation: if a template has multiple dynamic fields, merge them into a single contiguous block (e.g., serialize {user_id}|{timestamp}|{session_flag} as one unit), align that block to a boundary, and treat everything before it as a static monolith — this converts M poisoned blocks into one, recovering (M-1) blocks of cache. The harder tradeoff emerges with semantic padding: stuffing the gap with meaningful but generic text (e.g., filler instructions) rather than blank tokens can slightly degrade model behavior because the model attends to that content, whereas pure whitespace padding is semantically inert but may shift tokenization in unexpected ways depending on the tokenizer (BPE tokenizers often merge whitespace runs, collapsing your carefully measured padding). A less obvious cost is cache key stability: if your padding content ever varies — even a version string in a comment — you re-poison the blocks you were trying to protect, so alignment strategies require operational discipline to maintain, and any prompt templating system that allows ad-hoc edits to the "static" region will silently destroy cache efficiency in production.

In multi-tenant deployments the prefix cache becomes a shared resource with no tenant-level ownership, so two tenants whose prompts share a 800-token system prompt but diverge at token 801 with conflicting dynamic content will both try to claim the same radix-tree root — this is fine for reads, but when the cache is memory-pressured and an eviction policy must choose which divergent branch to drop, the loser pays full recompute cost on its next request, and under high concurrency this creates priority inversion: a high-frequency low-value tenant can crowd out a low-frequency high-value one simply by generating more cache activity. SGLang's RadixAttention uses an LRU eviction policy on the radix tree nodes, which means a branch that hasn't been accessed recently gets evicted regardless of its recompute cost — a 2000-token shared branch and a 20-token branch are treated identically by the eviction logic, which is a known limitation; cost-aware eviction (weighting nodes by KV size × expected reuse frequency) is discussed in the SGLang paper but not fully implemented in the original release. vLLM's block allocator handles divergence by reference-counting KV pages: a shared prefix page has refcount > 1 and is never evicted while any tenant holds a reference, but once all referencing sequences complete, the page becomes eviction-eligible immediately — meaning a burst of completed requests can simultaneously release a large shared prefix and cause a cold-cache episode for the next wave, a pattern that shows up as periodic latency spikes in production traces. In agentic settings the problem compounds because agents often mutate the "shared" context mid-flight — a tool-call result or memory write injected into what was a stable system prompt creates a cache fork: the pre-injection prefix is cacheable, but every agent instance that injected different tool results now has a unique branch, and the number of live branches scales with the number of concurrent agent instances, potentially exhausting GPU memory with partially-overlapping KV trees. The mitigation that production systems are converging on is tenant-aware scheduling: co-locating requests from the same tenant (or same agent lineage) on the same worker so their cache branches don't compete for the same physical pages — Mooncake (Qian et al., 2024) makes this explicit with a disaggregated KV cache architecture that separates prefill and decode workers and routes prefill requests by prefix hash to maximize locality, reporting up to 75% reduction in redundant KV computation in multi-tenant workloads.

A viral shared prefix creates a classic hot-shard problem: perfect prefix-hash routing concentrates all requests sharing that prefix onto one worker, which saturates its KV cache memory and request queue while others are underutilized, and the cache-hit benefit (avoiding recompute) is eventually outweighed by queueing delay as the hot worker backs up. The practical resolution is replication with threshold-based spillover: once a prefix's request rate exceeds some worker capacity fraction (say, the worker is >70% utilized), the scheduler promotes that prefix's KV cache to additional workers by explicitly copying or recomputing it there, accepting a one-time recompute cost to unlock horizontal scaling — this is essentially the approach described in DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024), which profiles per-prefix load and replicates KV state to secondary workers when a primary becomes a bottleneck. The key metric is the replication break-even point: copying a large KV cache (e.g., a 4096-token prefix at FP16 in a 70B model with 80 KV heads can be several GB) across NVLink or PCIe has non-trivial latency, so replication only pays off if the prefix will serve enough subsequent requests on the new worker to amortize the transfer cost before the next eviction — this break-even is typically tens to hundreds of requests depending on interconnect bandwidth. A lighter-weight alternative is consistent hashing with virtual nodes: rather than routing all requests for a prefix to one physical worker, you assign the prefix to a small replication group (e.g., 3 workers) and load-balance within that group, so cache hits are probabilistic (1/3 chance of hitting the right worker without recompute) but the hot-spot is spread — Llumnix (2024) implements dynamic request migration where requests in flight can be rescheduled to a less-loaded worker that then absorbs a cache miss, trading latency variance for throughput fairness. The deeper systems tension is that cache efficiency and load balance are fundamentally adversarial objectives: maximizing cache hit rate wants to concentrate similar requests, while maximizing load balance wants to disperse them, and the optimal operating point shifts dynamically with request arrival patterns — production systems like those at large inference providers reportedly tune the concentration-vs-balance tradeoff continuously using request rate signals, but published numbers on the exact policies remain sparse because this is a key competitive differentiator.

The failure mode is KV-weight mismatch: the KV cache stores materialized projections (W_K · x, W_V · x) computed under the old weight matrices, and if the decode steps run under new weights with different W_Q, the attention scores Q_new · K_old^T are geometrically meaningless — the dot products combine vectors from different learned subspaces, producing attention distributions that are neither the old model's nor the new model's, but an incoherent hybrid that typically manifests as degraded output quality, repetition, or incoherent completions rather than a hard crash, making it insidious to detect. The severity scales with how much the weights changed: a small LoRA adapter update that modifies only a fraction of layers may corrupt only the KV entries for those layers while leaving others valid, but even a 1% weight perturbation in early layers propagates forward through residual connections, meaning the "clean" upper-layer KV entries were computed from corrupted hidden states and are also invalid — there is no safe partial reuse across a weight update boundary. Production systems handle this by cache versioning: each KV cache entry is tagged with a (model_id, checkpoint_hash) tuple, and on any weight update the scheduler increments the version, causing all existing entries to be treated as cold misses on next access — vLLM and SGLang both implement a model fingerprint in their cache key, so a weight swap automatically invalidates the entire cache without requiring explicit flushes. The operational cost is a cold-start penalty proportional to the cache's working set: if a deployment has accumulated 50GB of warm KV cache for popular prefixes, a model update forces recomputing all of it on the next request wave, which can cause a transient latency spike of several minutes in high-traffic deployments before the cache warms back up. A subtler consistency problem arises with rolling updates — if you update workers one at a time to avoid downtime, requests during the transition window may hit old-weight workers or new-weight workers depending on routing, and a single multi-turn conversation whose prefill lands on an old worker but whose subsequent decode is migrated to a new worker will silently mix KV entries across weight versions, a race condition that versioned cache keys alone don't protect against without also pinning a conversation's full lifetime to a consistent model version.

Zero cache disruption is theoretically unachievable for any update that changes the projection matrices W_K or W_V, because the cached values are deterministic functions of those weights — there is no mathematical transformation that converts old KV entries to new ones without recomputing from token embeddings, unless the weight delta has special structure (e.g., a rank-1 update with a closed-form correction), which is never guaranteed in practice and hasn't been exploited in any production system to date. The closest practical approximation is blue-green deployment with session affinity: you spin up a complete parallel stack (new weights, empty cache) and route new conversations to it while existing conversations drain on the old stack, so no in-flight session ever crosses a weight boundary — the cache disruption is real but absorbed by the new stack's warm-up period rather than injected as a consistency race, and the old stack's cache is simply abandoned once all sessions drain, typically within minutes for stateless or short-context workloads. The warm-up latency on the new stack is the irreducible cost, and the standard mitigation is cache pre-warming: before shifting traffic, replay a sample of recent high-frequency prefixes through the new stack to populate its KV cache, so the cold-start spike is absorbed offline rather than on live traffic — Anthropic and similar providers reportedly use synthetic prefix replay during deployment ceremonies, though published specifics are scarce. For continuous fine-tuning scenarios (e.g., daily LoRA adapter refreshes), some systems exploit adapter-layer isolation: since LoRA modifies only a low-rank residual, you can checkpoint which transformer layers were modified and selectively invalidate only the KV entries for those layers, preserving cache entries for unmodified early layers — this is theoretically valid only if the modified layers don't affect earlier layers' hidden states, which holds for LoRA applied to attention output projections but breaks for updates to embedding or early MLP layers. The irreducible consistency window is therefore bounded by session drain time plus pre-warm time, and the honest engineering answer is that zero disruption is replaced by bounded and predictable disruption: blue-green with pre-warming can reduce the user-visible cold-cache penalty to the first few hundred requests on the new stack, which for high-traffic deployments is seconds of elevated latency rather than minutes, and that is the practical state of the art.

Per-tenant LoRA multiplexing collapses the shared prefix cache in the general case: the KV entries for a prefix are functions of (base weights + adapter weights), so tenant A's adapter and tenant B's adapter produce different KV tensors for identical input tokens, meaning the "shared" prefix cache must actually be partitioned by (prefix_hash, adapter_id) — the cache that looked like one hot entry for a popular system prompt becomes N separate entries, one per tenant adapter, each requiring independent storage and recompute. Punica (Chen et al., 2023) is the canonical system for batched LoRA serving and explicitly confronts this: it uses CUDA kernels that apply different LoRA deltas to different sequences in the same batch, but its KV cache is per-sequence because there is no cross-tenant prefix sharing once adapters diverge — the system essentially abandons shared prefix caching as a feature in exchange for adapter flexibility. The memory arithmetic is punishing: if a popular 1000-token system prompt generates a KV cache entry of ~500MB for a 70B model, and you have 1000 tenants with distinct adapters, naive per-(prefix, adapter) caching requires 500GB just for that one prefix — which is why S-LoRA (Sheng et al., 2023) introduces a tiered storage system that keeps adapter weights in CPU memory and streams them to GPU on demand, but still doesn't solve the KV cache explosion, instead accepting cache misses as the price of memory feasibility. The only structural escape is adapter-invariant prefix caching: if you can guarantee that a tenant's LoRA adapter is applied only to layers above some depth d, then KV entries for layers 0…d-1 are identical across all tenants sharing that adapter-free prefix, and you can cache that partial prefix once — this requires disciplined adapter design (no modifications to embedding or early attention layers) and a serving runtime that materializes KV layer-by-layer rather than all-at-once, which is non-standard but architecturally feasible. The sharpest operational implication is that multi-tenant LoRA serving forces a cache granularity decision at system design time: coarse caching (per full prefix) gives high hit rates only for tenants sharing identical adapters, while fine-grained layer-wise caching recovers sharing for adapter-free layers but adds cache management complexity that scales with the number of layers times the number of distinct adapters — and no major open-source serving system has fully implemented the layer-wise path as of early 2025.
